nameStory: Rim lichen gets its name from the distinctive raised rim or border that typically surrounds its disc-shaped reproductive structures called apothecia. The species name 'subimmergens' means 'somewhat sunken,' referring to how its apothecia sit partially embedded in the lichen's crusty body, creating that characteristic rimmed appearance.
description: Rim lichen is a crusty, rock-hugging lichen that forms thin patches directly on stone surfaces. It creates a grayish to whitish crust that can spread several inches across rock faces, looking almost like someone splattered pale paint that dried and cracked. The lichen is most noticeable when its small, disc-like reproductive structures appear, each surrounded by a lighter-colored rim that gives this group its common name. Individual colonies can persist for decades, slowly expanding across suitable rock surfaces.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Forms a thin, crusty coating that's tightly bonded to rock surfaces - you can't peel it off like you might with leafy lichens

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Exclusively grows on rock surfaces, particularly favoring hard stones like granite or quartzite that weather slowly

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels rough and gritty to the touch, like fine sandpaper, and often develops a network of small cracks as it ages

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Appears grayish-white to pale gray when dry, may darken slightly and look more vivid when wet from rain or morning dew

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Produces small, round, disc-like apothecia that sit partially sunken into the crusty body, each with a pale rim around a darker center

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Individual patches can spread 2-6 inches across, though multiple colonies often merge to cover much larger rock surfaces

habitat: Look for rim lichen on exposed rock outcrops, stone walls, and large boulders throughout New England's forests and open areas. It particularly favors acidic rocks like granite and avoids limestone or other basic rocks. You'll often find it on rocks that get some direct sunlight but aren't completely sun-baked all day.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more noticeable as spring rains darken and intensify its colors, making the contrast between the crusty body and any reproductive structures more obvious.
seasonality.summer: May appear faded and chalky during dry spells, but maintains its basic structure and identifying features throughout the season.
seasonality.fall: Autumn moisture helps revive colors, and this is often when apothecia are most visible and well-developed for identification.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow and looks particularly striking against white backgrounds, though wet winter conditions may make colors appear more muted.

funFact: This lichen is a true world traveler - scientists have found essentially identical rim lichen growing on rocks across three different continents, from Asian mountains to Australian outcrops, suggesting it's been hitchhiking around the globe far longer than humans have been keeping track!
confusionNotes: Can be confused with other crusty rock lichens, but most lack the distinctive partially-sunken apothecia with pale rims. Remember: if you can easily peel it off the rock, it's probably not a rim lichen - these are committed rock-huggers that bond permanently to their stone homes.
contextualKnowledge: With only one recorded observation in New England, this lichen is either extremely rare in our region or significantly under-reported by citizen scientists. Many crusty rock lichens require microscopic examination for definitive identification, so there may be more rim lichen out there than records suggest.
compareHints: Unlike its more common relatives like Common Rim Lichen which often grows on tree bark, rim lichen is strictly a rock specialist. It differs from Granite-speck Rim Lichen by having larger, more obvious apothecia, and from Sunken Rim-lichen by having apothecia that are only partially (not completely) embedded in the crusty body. The key is looking for those characteristic rimmed discs sitting partway down into the lichen's surface.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Pink-eyed White-rim stands out from its Lecanora relatives by its distinctive pink to reddish-brown apothecia with white rims - most other rim lichens in the genus have brown, black, or yellow reproductive discs.
Among the rim lichens in its genus, Mapledust Lichen stands out for its distinctly dusty, powdery surface texture.
Among its rim-lichen relatives, Mealy Rim-lichen is distinguished by its distinctly granular, powdery surface texture.
Among its rim lichen relatives, Bumpy Rim-lichen stands out for having the most prominently raised fruiting bodies - they truly stick up from the surface rather than sitting flush with it.
Unlike its rim lichen relatives that prefer rock or bark, Driftwood Rim-lichen is uniquely specialized for weathered wood substrates.

Frosted Rim-lichen stands out from its Lecanora relatives by maintaining a consistently pale, whitish color rather than the grayer tones of Common Rim Lichen or the more yellowish hues of some other species in the genus.
Unlike many of its rim lichen relatives that grow on tree bark or soil, Granite-speck Rim Lichen is almost exclusively rock-dwelling.
Beaded Rim-lichen differs from its many Lecanora relatives primarily through its distinctive beaded apothecia rims - most other rim lichens in the genus have smooth, clean rim edges.

Unlike Common Rim Lichen which has prominent raised apothecia, or Granite-speck Rim Lichen which tends to form more scattered, speckled patterns, Sunken Rim-lichen's defining characteristic is those distinctive crater-like depressions.
Among its rim lichen relatives, Dusted White-Rim stands out for its distinctly powdery surface texture, while species like Common Rim Lichen tend to have smoother surfaces.
Among its rim lichen relatives, this species tends to prefer more acidic substrates compared to Common Rim Lichen, which grows on more neutral bark.
Unlike the more common Granite-speck Rim Lichen which has a smoother surface, Lecanora intricata has that distinctive granular texture.

**Uncertain comparison warning** Among its Lecanora relatives, Common Rim Lichen is distinguished by its preference for exposed rock (unlike bark-dwelling species like Mealy Rim-lichen) and its particularly well-defined raised rims around the apothecia.
Unlike the Common Rim Lichen which has clearly separate, well-defined disc structures, Fused Rim Lichen's reproductive bodies appear to merge together.
